title: Sequencing 101: Structural variation
summary: Learn what structural variants are, the main types, why they matter in human health and agriculture, and how HiFi sequencing finds the SVs short reads miss.
body_markdown:
Updated November 2026 · Originally published December 2023


Over the last 50 years, the field of genetics has made monumental leaps, from the invention of DNA sequencing to the completion of the Human Genome Project and the emergence of genomic medicine. Yet many secrets remain hidden in the genome, and a large share of them sit in structural variation: the deletions, insertions, duplications, inversions, and rearrangements of 50 base pairs or more that drive rare disease, cancer, and trait diversity. With highly accurate long reads, researchers can now detect these structural variants directly instead of inferring them.


If you’re not sure whether short reads are missing structural variants in your research, our new guide covers why long reads matter for SVs, the latest evidence, and a seven-step checklist from DNA extraction to analysis.


[Explore the guide](https://programs.pacb.com/l/1652/2026-10-26/45nxk1)


## What is structural variation?


---


****Structural variants (SVs) are variations in DNA sequences from one individual to another that range anywhere from as little as 50 to more than a million base pairs in size.****


Since the inception of DNA sequencing in 1977, one could argue that the focus in genetics and genomics has been on the subtleties of single-base-pair differences or single nucleotide variants (SNVs). The often-cited claims that any two human genomes are 99.9% identical, or that humans and chimpanzees share 99% of their DNA, come from this “single nucleotide view” of genomics.1,2 SVs, on the other hand, cast a much broader net. These genomic variants encompass a diverse spectrum of genetic changes on a grand scale, including inversions, balanced translocations, and insertions and deletions. The latter two can lead to genomic imbalances known as copy number variants (CNVs). CNVs are regions of DNA where the number of copies of a gene or segment of DNA can differ between individuals. When such CNVs are present in more than 1% of a population they are deemed to be copy number polymorphisms (CNPs).3


But the significance of SVs extends far beyond what we currently know. In this evolving research landscape, the challenge lies in uncovering and fully understanding the extent of structural variation, as well as in routinely genotyping these diverse genetic changes. Structural variation remains one of the least explored areas of genetics, with implications for a wide range of topics, from human disease and complex traits to the evolution and diversification of life itself.


## What are the different types of structural variation?


---


SVs take many forms. The most recognized types of structural variants include:


- ****Insertions**** : New genetic material is added into the genome, introducing novel sequences.
- ****Deletions**** : Portions of the genetic code are missing or deleted, leading to an altered DNA sequence.
- ****Duplications**** : Certain DNA segments are duplicated, resulting in multiple copies of similar genetic material.
- ****Inversions**** : Genetic regions are flipped or inverted, causing changes in the order of nucleotide bases.
- ****Translocations**** : DNA sequences are exchanged between different chromosomes, leading to new combinations of genetic material.
- ****Copy number variants (CNVs)**** : Regions of the genome where the number of copies may vary among individuals, giving rise to genomic imbalances.
- ****Complex rearrangements**** : Combinations of gains, losses, and rearrangements at one locus, such as ring and marker chromosomes.

Together, these SVs are thought to be the grand architects of genetic diversity, contributing to the complexity, richness, and diversity of life on earth. They can also be the root cause of various genetic diseases in humans, underscoring their importance in biomedical research as well.


## **Why is structural variation important?**


---


The study of structural variation is an exciting domain in genetics and genomics with potentially far-reaching implications for human health, agriculture, and our fundamental understanding of biology. Perhaps unsurprisingly, there is growing evidence that much of the genetic variation housed within a population exists at a structural level in the genome.4, 5


### **The influence of structural variants on phenotype**


One of the most intriguing aspects of SVs is their capacity to exert an observable impact on an organism’s phenotype. SVs have been shown to disrupt or alter gene function, modify gene regulatory mechanisms, and even recalibrate gene dosage.6 Multiple studies have cast a spotlight on the pivotal role of SVs in driving functional changes across populations and species.2,7 At the same time, SVs’ influence on molecular biology and medicine is becoming increasingly evident. For example, in neurological diseases, SVs have been implicated in Parkinson’s disease with expansion of ATTCC repeats.8 Similarly, the elongation of CAG sequences at the scale of SVs has been tied to Huntington’s disease9. Additionally, a retrotransposon insertion within the *TAF1* gene has been linked to the preliminary stages of dystonia-parkinsonism disease.10 In the context of cancer, a variety of SVs have been identified as culprits, encompassing gene deletions or rearrangements, gene amplifications, gene fusions, and the reshuffling of gene regulatory elements.11, 12, 13


### **The influence of structural variation on plants and Mendelian disorders in humans**


In Mendelian genetics, SVs are proving to have a major impact on various diseases associated with deletions or duplications within genetic regions. For instance, complicated SVs affecting genes such as *ARID1B* (associated with Coffin-Siris syndrome) and *CDKL5* (associated with early infantile epileptic encephalopathy and Rett-like features) have been observed.14 These SVs can result in severe intellectual disability. Of course, it seems likely that most SVs are not strictly deleterious for humans. A pangenome analysis of the human Y chromosome published in the journal *Nature* revealed that, from individual to individual, Y chromosome size can vary by nearly two-fold. More importantly, low levels of base substitution observed in the analysis suggest that most variation in the Y is structural in nature.15


Agricultural research has also helped reveal the importance of SVs, where they have been shown to play a pivotal role in shaping phenotypes. SVs can confer tolerance to adverse conditions and positively impact crop yields and quality. For instance, SVs have been associated with aluminum resistance in maize, boron toxicity tolerance in barley, and glyphosate resistance in weeds.16, 17, 18 Furthermore, they have been linked to enhanced fruit yield and quality in plants like tomatoes.19


Despite their increasingly recognized importance, SVs have remained less explored, especially in comparison to SNVs. The main challenge in studying SVs stems from the difficulty in identifying them, given their large and often intricate patterns within the genome and their association with repetitive sequences in genomes. This complexity is further compounded by sequencing and mapping errors, along with the similar patterns that different types of SVs can produce. Furthermore, the challenge is intensified by the presence of overlapping or nested SVs, which further obscure the genomic landscape. However, highly accurate long-read sequencing technologies like PacBio[HiFi sequencing](https://www.pacb.com/technology/hifi-sequencing/) now make SV research a whole lot easier.


## Why short reads miss structural variants


Structural variants encompass more of the genome than any other type of variation,20 yet short-read sequencing misses many of them. Reads of a few hundred bases rarely span an SV, so short-read callers infer SVs indirectly from read pairs, split reads, and changes in read depth. That approach struggles in repeats, segmental duplications, and paralogous genes, which is exactly where many SVs occur. In a HiFi assembly panel of 171,233 SVs, two-thirds (66.0%) sat in tandem repeat regions.21 And across four genomes, short reads found roughly 13,000 SVs per genome against about 25,000 with long reads, missing about half of the long-read SVs.22


HiFi reads span each SV from breakpoint to breakpoint, so junctions and inserted sequence are read directly rather than inferred. Because HiFi reads are both long and highly accurate, they also resolve complete SVs in repeats and paralogous genes, phase variants into haplotypes, and capture SNVs, indels, SVs, CNVs, tandem repeats, and methylation from a single genome.


## What recent publications reveal about structural variants


A wave of recent studies has put long-read and short-read sequencing to the test in detecting structural variants and, notably, used HiFi sequencing to resolve SVs that earlier tests could not.


### **Rare disease and human genetics**


- ****Marker chromosomes**** : HiFi genomes resolved 9 of 10 supernumerary marker chromosomes to base-pair junctions, where short reads resolved 2 of 8.23
- ****Hidden deletions**** : HiFi genomes found homozygous *TANGO2* deletions of ~33.8 kb and ~9.4 kb that trio exome and microarray had missed.24
- ****Autism**** : In 267 people with autism, long-read genomes detected 33% more gene-disrupting SVs than short reads, and 16,488 novel SVs appeared only in long reads, against 7,084 only in short reads.25
- ****Clinically relevant variants**** : Of 70 hard-to-detect variants tested on both platforms, HiFi genomes automatically detected 89% and short-read genomes 41%.26


### **Cancer**


- ****Pediatric leukemia**** : In 4 of 12 children, HiFi sequencing detected somatic SV drivers that defined a genetic subtype routine clinical testing had missed.27


### **Agriculture**


- ****Peanut breeding**** : In a peanut MAGIC population, HiFi low-pass sequencing with a pangenome graph detected 2.7× as many large SVs (>1 kb) per sample as short reads.28


## **How to detect and analyze structural variants with HiFi sequencing**


---


HiFi sequencing has breathed new life into SV research. Its capability to generate long (typically 15–20 kb) and highly accurate (Q30+) reads has made the detection and analysis of SVs significantly more accessible for researchers, on the Revio system for high-throughput projects and the Vega benchtop system for smaller studies. This long-read technology can also be used for complementary approaches including[Kinnex full-length transcriptomics](https://www.pacb.com/products-and-services/applications/rna-sequencing/) that enable the identification of functional SVs through the detection of alternative splicing and RNA fusions.


The[PacBio WGS Variant Pipeline](https://github.com/PacificBiosciences/HiFi-human-WGS-WDL) takes unaligned HiFi reads to phased variant calls in one workflow:[pbmm2](https://github.com/PacificBiosciences/pbmm2) aligns reads,[sawfish](https://github.com/PacificBiosciences/sawfish) calls SVs and copy number variants together, and[HiPhase](https://github.com/PacificBiosciences/HiPhase) phases them with small variants and tandem repeats. At 15× coverage, sawfish matched the accuracy that other long-read SV callers needed at least 30× coverage to reach.29 Beyond the pipeline,[SVTopo](https://github.com/PacificBiosciences/SVTopo) draws complex rearrangements, and the[CoLoRSdb](https://colorsdb.org/) long-read catalog helps filter out common SVs.


With better detection methods and ongoing work on benchmarking and quality control standards, researchers are well positioned to uncover the many hidden aspects of structural variation and its impact on the living world.


## **Taking the next step in SV research**


---


The best place to start is with the samples short reads left negative or ambiguous. You already know the question, so you can measure exactly what HiFi adds. Our guide walks through a seven-step checklist, from planning coverage to calling, phasing, and visualizing SVs.
